title: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon
shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon
summary: Launch Daemons are the system-wide counterpart to Launch Agents. They are property list files read by launchd from /System/Library/LaunchDaemons and /Library/LaunchDaemons, and unlike agents they are loaded before anyone logs in and run on behalf of every user. Installing one requires elevated privileges, and the program it names inherits administrative rights, which is exactly why the technique appears in macOS malware that wants a durable, unprivileged-looking foothold with powerful execution. Detection focuses on the plist contents and the referenced executable rather than the plist alone. A daemon that sets RunAtLoad to true and points Program at a binary in a temporary directory, a hidden folder, or a world-writable location such as a globally writable usr/local/bin is suspicious, especially when the Label mimics Apple or a third-party vendor. A separate and easily missed variant does not add a daemon at all: because weak permissions can make a directory referenced by an existing daemon writable, an attacker simply replaces the legitimate executable that the daemon already launches. Comparing the contents of referenced programs against package manager records and code signature checks is therefore part of a complete review, alongside launchctl output and file integrity monitoring of the daemon directories.

beginner.definition: A Launch Daemon is a settings file on macOS that starts a program in the background for the whole computer. It runs before anyone logs in, and it does not need a user to be sitting at the machine. Apple uses daemons for shared services and updates.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker who can add a daemon gets their program running for every user, every time the Mac starts. The program runs with administrator rights, so it can do almost anything on that machine. Because daemons are normal Apple plumbing, a new one rarely looks out of place. It is a strong and lasting foothold.
howItWorks: The attacker needs administrator rights, because daemon files live in protected system folders.
They write a property list file naming their program, and place it in a LaunchDaemons folder.
The Label key names the job, and the Program key holds the path of the executable to run.
Setting RunAtLoad to true makes the program start as soon as the system loads daemons.
At startup, launchd reads the file and starts the program with administrative rights.
A weaker variant replaces the program an existing daemon already points to, which adds no new file.
beginner.example: Picture an office building with a facilities cupboard and a folder of standing instructions. Each instruction tells the caretaker to switch something on at six each morning. Someone adds a page telling the caretaker to unlock a specific storage room first, and signs it like a normal company memo. The caretaker follows it daily, before any staff arrive.
takeaways: Launch Daemons are system-wide and start before login, unlike per-user Launch Agents.
They need administrator rights to install but give the attacker the same level of access back.
Also check the programs existing daemons point to, because a weak folder permission allows swapping them.

objectives: Explain how a Launch Daemon differs from a Launch Agent.
Describe the launchd startup sequence and when daemons load.
Name the required plist keys for a Launch Daemon.
Explain why daemon installation requires elevated privileges.
Describe the risk of writable folders that daemons already reference.
